newsitem.title: UK: Robust emerging market bond supply set to continue.
newsitem.headline: Robust emerging market bond supply set to continue.

text.p: Increased confidence in emerging market credits resulted in more than a 60 percent increase of international bond issuance from the sector in the first half of 1997 versus the same period last year, bankers said on Tuesday.
A significant improvement was noted in credit ratings, an increase in the size of issues, a lengthening in the maturities of bonds and a broader distribution of paper, bankers said.

Syndicate officials cited a number of impressive ground-breaking transactions that were launched this year -- among them Russia's $2.0 billion 10-year bond, Brazil's 30-year Brady swap as well as its "parallel" bond, the first such deal in preparation of the planned euro for an emerging market borrower.
Added to this there were many sovereign debut Eurobonds; among them the cities of Moscow and St Petersburg, Croatia, Cyprus, Ecuador, Jamaica, Moldova and Panama.
Fears of further U.S. raising interest rates have been abated with at the most a half-point rate rise being mooted, dealers said.
"The international interest rate environment has been conducive to the launch of high-yielding paper as investors continue the hunt for spread," ING Barings syndicate official Stephen Taber said.
Volume of emerging market supply totalled almost $58 billion in the first six months of this year versus almost $36 billion for the same period last year, Capital DATA Bondware showed.

Almost half of the volume this year was shown to be from Latin American borrowers, at almost $27 billion. Eastern European supply showed the greatest pick-up -- $1.1 billion in the first half of 1996 to $6.2 billion this half-year.
The volume for the emerging market sector for 1996 as a whole was almost $85 billion versus $45 billion in 1995.
"The first six months' paper has been absorbed so generally it all is positive," SBC Warburg director Dermot Mayes said.
General consensus was that supply from Eastern Europe would continue to flourish as the region sought to diversify funding at attractive levels.
Issuance from the Russian region was expected to continue to surge, they said.
ABN AMRO syndicate official Ronnie Rana said he expected a resurgence of emerging market currency supply "like the Czech crown and Polish zloty".
Added to this, ANZ research analyst Neil Lockwood said Russia was expected to be upgraded in the third quarter of this year.
While the dollar sector continued the most favoured, issuance in the mark sector was expected to pick-up especially for eastern European borrowers wanting to tap the European investor base.

The only concerns voiced were whether demand would continue and whether spreads could continue to tighten at the rate they had been, with some saying their naturally cynically side cautioned them to get too comfortable.

However the quality of the investor base was said to be better-informed, and emerging market funds were becoming more global enabling them to purchase more paper which augured well for the future, bankers said.
